pronunciation.approximation: foo-shee, rising tone on fu, high level on xi.
pronunciation.note: Fúxī 伏羲 carries the rising tone on fú and the high level tone on xī in Mandarin; older romanizations write Fu-hsi. The first graph 伏 suggests "to subdue, to prostrate," the second 羲 a sacrificial term — a name older than its etymologies, borne by the first of the Three August Ones. The older romanization Fu-hsi records the same syllables; pinyin's x is the alveolo-palatal fricative of modern Mandarin.

domains.title: The First Teacher
domains.subtitle: The Eight Trigrams, the Net, and the Marriage on the Mountain
domains.lead: Fúxī is where Chinese civilization says it learned to think: the sage-king who looked up at the heavens, down at the earth, and at the markings on birds and beasts — and abstracted the eight trigrams, the first writing of pattern itself.

cards.name: The Eight Trigrams
cards.desc: Bāguà: broken and unbroken lines in threes — the binary alphabet of the Yìjīng, attributed to his observation.

cards.name: The Net
cards.desc: He taught the people to knot cords into nets — fishing, hunting, and the technology of the snare.

cards.name: The Serpent Bodies
cards.desc: Han art shows him and Nǚwā as serpents intertwined — the primal pair, measuring square and compass in hand.

cards.name: Marriage
cards.desc: He instituted the rites of marriage and the bride-price of deer skins — order after the flood.

symbols.name: The trigrams
symbols.meaning: Pattern abstracted from nature — the seed of all Chinese correlative thought

symbols.name: The carpenter's square
symbols.meaning: His emblem in Han art: the earth-measurer's tool (Nǚwā holds the compass of heaven)

symbols.name: The dragon-horse
symbols.meaning: The creature from the Yellow River whose markings revealed the diagram

mythology.lead: Fúxī's myths are all acts of notation: he does not fight or flee — he observes, abstracts, and teaches. He is the culture-bringer as draftsman.

myths.title: Reading the World
myths.text: The Yìjīng's Great Treatise records the founding act: Fúxī looked up and contemplated the images of heaven, looked down and contemplated the patterns of earth, contemplated the markings of birds and beasts and the order of the near at hand — and from all three made the eight trigrams, "to comprehend the powers of the spirits and to classify the natures of the ten thousand things." Writing, mathematics, and divination begin as one gesture of attention.

myths.title: The Dragon-Horse's Map
myths.text: Later tradition gives the revelation a courier: a dragon-horse rose from the Yellow River bearing on its back the Hétú, the River Chart — the arrangement of numbers and marks from which Fúxī drew the trigrams. Paired with the Luò River Writing that inspired the Great Plan, the Chart made the Yellow River itself the first text of Chinese civilization.

myths.title: The Brother-Sister Marriage
myths.text: In the flood myth recorded among the Miao and in Tang collections, Fúxī and Nǚwā alone survive the waters, taking refuge on Mount Kūnlún. Brother and sister, they divine heaven's will by rolling millstones and watching smoke columns join — and consent to marry, repopulating the drowned world. The myth explains both marriage's institution and humanity's second beginning.

myths.title: Nets, Music, and Domestication
myths.text: The tradition credits him with the survival-arts in sequence: knotting cords into nets for fishing and hunting, keeping domestic animals (hence one reading of his name, "subduer of beasts"), making the thirty-five-stringed se zither, and fixing the marriage rites. Civilization, in his legend, is a curriculum — and he is its whole faculty.

lore.syncretism: He heads most lists of the Three August Ones (Sānhuáng), paired inseparably with Nǚwā — their intertwined serpent forms in Han art echoing, scholars note, the union of measure and generation. Daoist tradition absorbed him as a revealer of the trigrams to the immortal lineages; Confucian tradition kept him as the first historian of pattern. The serpent-pair iconography has been compared by art historians with intertwined pairs from Egypt to India — diffusion debated, the resemblance celebrated.
lore.culturalLegacy: Every reading of the Yìjīng — the book that shaped Confucian statecraft, Daoist alchemy, and Leibniz's binary arithmetic — begins with his act of looking. The eight trigrams appear on the flag of South Korea; the River Chart structures a millennium of cosmological diagrams; and "Fúxī" remains the standard icon for the inventor-ancestor in Chinese cultural memory, the answer to the question of where pattern-thinking began.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Fúxī is the patron of the second look — the one that sees not the thing but the pattern. His trigrams are only broken and unbroken lines, yet a civilization read everything in them for three thousand years. He asks the observer's question: what in the world are you willing to look at long enough that it begins, at last, to read back?

Leibniz saw the trigrams and recognized binary arithmetic; the information age looked again and found the whole grammar of bits — the broken and unbroken line as zero and one. Whether or not the old sage intended the code, his lesson stands: the world's patterns are legible to whoever looks long enough, and three lines, honestly observed, can hold a civilization's worth of distinctions. The first technology was attention.

The tradition says he looked at the horse's markings and the turtle's shell and saw not omen but order — the world already written, waiting for a reader. Every analysis since, from the Yìjīng's commentaries to the database schema, is his gesture repeated: reduce the world to its honest marks, and the marks will begin to answer.
lore.archaeology: The Wu Liang shrine reliefs (2nd century CE, Shandong) show Fúxī and Nǚwā with serpent bodies entwined, square and compass raised — the canonical image, replicated across Han tomb art from Sichuan to Xinjiang (the famous Astana cemetery banner). The myth's textual archaeology runs from the Zhuangzi and Xunzi mentions to the Tang's flood-cycle records: a steady accretion from sage-king to cosmic progenitor, all preserved in the transmitted classics.
lore.originalScriptNote: Written 伏羲: fú (subdue; the man-radical with the hound) plus xī (the ancient graph for sacrificial breath). The compound is attested from Warring States texts onward — the name predates any agreed reading of it, which is itself a mark of antiquity.
